extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers interested in poetry, drama, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: A Spectator-style periodical essay giving critical standards for epic poetry (Milton's Paradise Lost), theatrical performance, and social virtues (modesty/assurance). It mixes literary evaluation with practical recommendations for the stage and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poem should end happily
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem...ought to end happily, and leave the Mind of the Reader, after having conducted it through many Doubts and Fears, Sorrows and Disquietudes, in a State of Tranquility and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton supplies this by representing the Adversary in mortification and the first Parents comforted by Dreams and Visions; the happy ending restores reader's tranquility and is a necessary qualification of heroic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate epic under four heads: Fable, Characters, Sentiments, Language
rubrics_metrics.description: The author takes a general view of the poem under these four Heads, and confines censure and praise within them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify merits and blemishes; each head can contain many specific kinds of beauty or fault (e.g., invention under Characters, diction under Language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic should embody a universal moral (deducible but not primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: No just Heroick Poem ever was or can be made, from whence one great Moral may not be deduced; yet an Epick Writer does not first pitch upon a certain Moral as the ground-work and then find a Story to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great moral (e.g., 'Obedience to the Will of God makes Men happy') should be visible in the fable, but the moral must arise naturally from the story, not be imposed beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use poetical ornaments where the subject permits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Narration rises very happily on several Occasions, where the Subject is capable of Poetical Ornaments, as particularly in the Confusion which he describes among the Builders of Babel, and in his short Sketch of the Plagues of Egypt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject lends itself to poetical decoration (sublime scenes, plagues, storms), embellish with appropriate imagery and ornament; avoid forcing ornament into unsuitable passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance theological/divine attention with poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: If Milton's Poem flags any where, it is in this Narration, where in some places the Author has been so attentive to his Divinity, that he has neglected his Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow dense theological exposition to disrupt poetic invention and diction; preserve poetic qualities even when handling divine or doctrinal material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions should be strong and vivid
rubrics_metrics.description: The Storm of Hail and Fire, with the Darkness that overspread the Land for three Days, are described with great Strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forceful, muscular description is praiseworthy for dramatic natural events; strive for energetic diction in scenes of catastrophe or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of scriptural allusion and direct biblical imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The River-Dragon is an Allusion to the Crocodile...This Allusion is taken from that Sublime Passage in Ezekiel...Milton has given us another very noble and poetical Image...which is copied almost Word for Word out of the History of Moses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural allusions and even verbatim echoes can enrich imagery and authority when used judiciously and nobly; they lend weight and familiarity in a religiously themed epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make visionary episodes lively with concrete particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Angel is described as seeing the Patriarch actually travelling towards the Land of Promise, which gives a particular Liveliness to this part of the Narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting visions of future persons/events, include concrete, particular details (places, tents, trains) to enliven the scene and increase verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical models (Virgil/Homer) as legitimate hints
rubrics_metrics.description: As Virgil's Vision in the sixth Æneid probably gave Milton the Hint of this whole Episode...The last Line is a Translation of that Verse, where Anchises mentions the Names of Places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical imitation or translation can provide structural and rhetorical models; emulate virtues from Homer/Virgil while adapting to English poetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray antagonist's downfall and protagonist's consolation for moral closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan is represented miserable in the height of his Triumphs, and Adam triumphant in the height of Misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast the defeated grandeur of the adversary with the restored or hopeful state of the protagonist to achieve moral and emotional resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with moral and instructive speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: The last Speeches of Adam and the Arch-Angel are full of Moral and Instructive Sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings that include clear, consoling, and didactic speeches (without spoiling poetry) leave the reader with pleasure and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sleep and dreams as consolatory poetic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sleep that fell upon Eve, and the Effects it had in quieting the Disorders of her Mind, produces the same kind of Consolation in the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dreams or gentle sleep-scenes to resolve inner turmoil, provide prophetic consolation, or transition the emotional tone toward peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure epic into books for just and regular disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Number of Books in Paradise Lost is equal to those of the Æneid...This second Division was made with great Judgment...for the more just and regular Disposition of this great Work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide a long epic into books/sections to improve pacing and organization; structural divisions should serve the poem's disposition rather than mere imitation of a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain temporal coherence where applicable; allow exception for supernatural action
rubrics_metrics.description: From Adam's first Appearance in the fourth Book, to his Expulsion from Paradise in the twelfth, the Author reckons ten Days. As for that part of the Action which is described in the three first Books...it is not subject to any Calculations of Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep earthly action temporally coherent for readers' comprehension; accept that metaphysical or supernatural scenes may transcend ordinary chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify types of poetic beauty and their sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Passages are beautiful by being Sublime, others by being Soft, others by being Natural; which of them are recommended by the Passion, which by the Moral, which by the Sentiment, and which by the Expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing, classify beauties (sublime, soft, natural) and understand whether they arise from passion, moral content, sentiment, or mere expression to better craft or judge passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should be suppressed or judiciously encouraged based on moral influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A Stage ought to be wholly suppressed, or judiciously encouraged...it is, with me, a Matter of the highest Consideration what Parts are well or ill performed, what Passions or Sentiments are indulged or cultivated, and consequently what Manners and Customs are transfused from the Stage to the World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote theatre when it polishes public taste and manners; discourage it when it disseminates vice or deformity of character. Evaluate productions by their moral and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors' portrayals can instruct public manners; choose parts that correct vices
rubrics_metrics.description: When I am commending Wilks for representing the Tenderness of a Husband...I talk to all the World who are engaged in any of those Circumstances...a well-regulated Stage would have upon Men's Manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should perform characters that exemplify virtues or expose follies; effective performance can cultivate public taste and shame social vices into retreat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach dancers and train gesture/motion in actors
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be a great Improvement, as well as Embellishment to the Theatre, if Dancing were more regarded, and taught to all the Actors...An amiable Modesty in one Aspect of a Dancer, an assumed Confidence in another...would revive in the Company all the fine Touches of Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate dance, refined gesture, and studied motion into performances to convey nuanced emotions and improve audience refinement; train actors in movement as well as speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of definitions to avoid abuse of moral words
rubrics_metrics.description: A Definition...is the only way whereby the precise Meaning of Moral Words can be known...he accuses those of great Negligence, who Discourse of Moral things with the least Obscurity in the Terms they make use of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and critical discourse, define key terms (e.g., 'modesty', 'assurance') to prevent confusion and inconsistent application of praise or blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty defined and recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty: The Reflection of an Ingenuous Mind, either when a Man has committed an Action for which he censures himself, or fancies that he is exposed to the Censure of others...A Man truly Modest is as much so when he is alone as in Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate self-reflection and sensitivity to one's faults; modesty is constant, private as well as public, and manifests in an internal readiness to censure oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance defined and recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance: the Faculty of possessing a Man's self, or of saying and doing indifferent things without any Uneasiness or Emotion in the Mind...what generally gives a Man Assurance is a moderate Knowledge of the World, but above all a Mind fixed and determined in it self to do nothing against the Rules of Honour and Decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage composed self-possession grounded in knowledge and steadfast moral resolve; assurance enables a person to bear misinterpretation and minor censure with dignity.
